description: Bring map reading, field observation, graphic logs and geological histories together to investigate a real area.
content_html:
This lesson covers general fieldwork skills required by the spec. Your school will have done specific fieldwork at a specific location — refer to your teacher's notes for your own examples and case-study data.

The Simplified Geological Map

Your written examination (the practical-skills component) is entirely based on a simplified geological map. Unlike the full 1:50,000 BGS maps used in professional work, the exam version uses a small number of named rock units, shows faults and fold axes clearly, and is accompanied by a cross-section framework and a stratigraphic column. The skills you need are: reading the map to identify rock types at any point, inferring structure from the map pattern, drawing or completing a cross-section, and constructing a sequence of geological events from the evidence shown.

Map reading is not passive. When you look at a simplified geological map, you should immediately ask: are the rock unit boundaries roughly parallel to the contours (horizontal strata), or do they cross contours (indicating dipping strata)? Are there any V-shaped bends in boundaries where a stream crosses them — and does the V point upstream (dipping downstream, as is most common) or downstream (dipping upstream, a steeper dip)? These V-patterns, combined with knowing the rule of Vs, allow you to infer the dip direction of strata before any other information is given.

Key Fact

The rule of Vs: when a geological boundary crosses a valley, horizontal strata produce a V-shape pointing upstream. Strata dipping downstream (with current) also point upstream, but the V is less sharp. Strata dipping upstream produce a V pointing downstream. Vertical strata show no V at all — the boundary crosses the valley in a straight line.

Constructing a Cross-Section

A geological cross-section shows what the geology looks like on a vertical slice through the Earth along a given line on the map. To construct one:

First, draw the topographic profile — plot the elevation at each point where a contour crosses your section line, then join the dots with a smooth curve. Next, mark where each geological boundary crosses the section line at the surface. Use the dip angles and directions given on the map (shown as dip arrows with the angle written beside them) to project boundaries downward into the subsurface at the correct angle. In exam answers, show the beds as parallel lines within each rock unit, continuing the boundary angles consistently. Faults are drawn as straight lines cutting across bedding at the correct dip, with the displacement clearly shown.

Constructing a geological history from a map is one of the highest-tariff skills in the practical-skills component. The method uses three principles in sequence: superposition (older rocks are below younger ones in an undisturbed sequence), cross-cutting relationships (any feature that cuts across another is younger: a fault cutting through bedding formed after the bedding; a dyke intruding across a fault formed after the fault), and unconformities (a surface of erosion representing a gap in the geological record, with younger horizontal beds resting on older tilted beds). Exam technique: state the events in order from oldest to youngest, use the names of the specific rock units shown on the map, and state the principle of evidence for each step. Do not just describe what you see — you must explain how the evidence leads to the conclusion.

Graphic Logs

A graphic log (or sedimentary log) is a vertical column drawn to scale showing the rock types and thicknesses encountered in a borehole or at an outcrop. Each rock type uses a standard symbol: dots for sandstone, dashes for mudstone, brick-pattern for limestone, and so on. Additional columns to the right record grain size (coarsening-up or fining-up sequences), fossils found at each level, and sedimentary structures such as cross-bedding or ripple marks. Reading a graphic log allows you to reconstruct the environment of deposition — alternating sandstones and mudstones suggest a fluctuating energy environment such as a tidal flat or delta margin; a thick uninterrupted limestone suggests a stable shallow marine environment.

In the field, a compass clinometer measures the dip angle and strike direction of rock surfaces such as bedding planes or fault planes. Strike is the compass direction of a horizontal line on the surface; dip is the maximum angle of inclination, measured perpendicular to strike. These values are plotted as dip arrows on a geological map. GPS is used to record the precise location of observations, ensuring measurements can be placed accurately on the map.

A rose diagram is a circular graph used to display directional data — for example, the strike directions of joints measured across an outcrop, or the orientation of pebble long-axes in a conglomerate. Petals on the rose represent the frequency of measurements in each compass direction. A rose diagram with two opposite petals suggests a single dominant joint set; one with four petals suggests two conjugate joint sets related to a tectonic stress field. In your exam, you may be asked to read a rose diagram and describe the dominant trend, or to explain what the pattern reveals about past stress or current flow directions.

Rock description in the field uses standardised language: for igneous rocks — colour, grain size (fine/medium/coarse), texture (porphyritic, vesicular, glassy), mineralogy (quartz, feldspar, mica as visible crystals). For sedimentary rocks — grain size, sorting, rounding, colour, sedimentary structures, fossil content. For metamorphic rocks — foliation (slate, schist) or banding (gneiss, but note gneiss is not on the spec; if in doubt, describe the texture without naming). Using only rock names that appear on the specification is essential for exam marks.

The Fieldwork Statement and Directed Investigation

The specification requires two field occasions before the exam, at least one of which must be a directed investigation — where you formulate a question, collect data systematically, and interpret your findings. There is no submitted portfolio; the fieldwork prepares you for examination questions that ask about field methods, data collection and interpretation. You may be asked to describe how you would carry out a field survey, what equipment you would use, how you would record data (field sketches, annotated drawings, written descriptions, graphic logs), and how you would process and present it (rose diagrams, cross-sections, geological histories).

Key Fact

Key fieldwork recording methods: field sketch (hand-drawn panoramic view of an outcrop with annotations for rock types, structures and features); annotated photograph (scaled photograph with labels identifying geological features); graphic log (scaled vertical column showing rock sequence and thicknesses); rose diagram (circular frequency plot of directional data). Each serves a different purpose and examiners may ask you to select and justify the most appropriate method for a given task.

The Geological Code of Conduct

All geological fieldwork in the UK is guided by the Geological Society's Geological Code of Conduct. Key principles include: always seeking permission from landowners before entering private land; working safely — never hammering at the base of an unstable face; collecting specimens minimally and only where legal; respecting other users of the countryside; and reporting significant new finds to geological bodies or local record centres. In your exam, if asked about responsible fieldwork, reference permission, safety and minimal impact — these are the three pillars the examiners look for.
exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark “Sequence Geological Events” question type in the practical-skills component, the most common error is describing what you see rather than sequencing what happened and when. Use the words “earliest” / “then” / “finally” to organise your answer, name the specific rock units from the map, and cite the principle of evidence for each step (superposition, cross-cutting, unconformity). For the cross-section question, use a ruler — examiners mark construction accuracy. Show all bedding planes as parallel lines within each unit and draw the fault at the angle indicated by the dip arrow.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • the practical-skills component is entirely map-based; key skills are applying the rule of Vs to infer dip direction, constructing cross-sections using surface data and dip angles, and sequencing geological events using superposition, cross-cutting and unconformities.
  • Graphic logs record rock sequences to scale; field tools include the compass clinometer (for dip and strike), GPS (for location), and rose diagrams (for directional data such as joint orientations).
  • Fieldwork requires two field occasions including at least one directed investigation; responsible practice follows the Geological Code of Conduct — permission, safety and minimal specimen collection.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes what a rose diagram shows?
A) The thickness of rock units in a borehole plotted to vertical scale
B) The frequency of measurements in different compass directions, shown as petals on a circular diagram
C) The relationship between grain size and depth in a sedimentary sequence
D) A vertical slice through the geology along a line drawn on a map
practice_questions.marks: B) The frequency of measurements in different compass directions, shown as petals on a circular diagram [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the combined field instrument used to measure both the strike and the dip of a rock surface.
Describe what a simplified geological map shows and state one way it differs from a professional BGS geological map.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for:
- A simplified geological map shows the surface distribution of rock units, their boundaries, faults and fold axes in a small exam-format area. (1)
- It uses fewer rock units and removes minor detail compared with the full-scale BGS 1:50,000 maps, making it manageable for exam use. (Accept other valid differences, e.g. scale, level of detail, number of units.) (1)

practice_questions.text: A geological map shows a rock boundary forming a V-shape that points downstream (in the direction water flows). What does this tell you about the dip direction of the strata? Explain your reasoning using the rule of Vs.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- The rule of Vs states that a boundary crossing a valley produces a V-shape pointing in the dip direction when beds are inclined, or pointing upstream for horizontal or gently downstream-dipping beds. (1)
- A V pointing downstream (against the normal upstream direction) indicates that the strata dip upstream — that is, into the hillside in the uphill direction. (1)
- This means the strata are dipping steeply enough in the upstream direction to produce a boundary that appears to lean against the valley gradient. (1)

practice_questions.text: A geological map shows the following sequence from bottom to top: mudstone, limestone (cut by a fault), sandstone unconformably overlying the limestone. Sequence these geological events from oldest to youngest, giving the evidence for each step.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each correctly evidenced step (up to 4):
1. Deposition of mudstone — oldest because it lies below all other units (superposition). (1)
2. Deposition of limestone above the mudstone — younger than the mudstone by superposition. (1)
3. Faulting of the limestone — the fault cuts the limestone so must post-date its deposition (cross-cutting relationships). (1)
4. Erosion followed by deposition of sandstone unconformably above the limestone — the unconformity represents a gap in the record; the sandstone is the youngest unit because it overlies all others (superposition). (1)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of fieldwork skills for understanding and interpreting a geological map in an examination context. Refer to specific skills and techniques in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly links specific fieldwork skills (compass clinometer, graphic logs, field sketches, rose diagrams) to map interpretation tasks; evaluates both the benefits and the limitations; reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: Discusses at least three specific skills with explanation of how they aid map interpretation; conclusion present.
Developing: Lists relevant skills but explanation of the link to map interpretation is limited; conclusion may be absent.
Emerging: Brief descriptive account of one or two skills without evaluative comment.

Key links between fieldwork and map interpretation:
- Compass clinometer use in the field teaches the student what dip angles feel like and how they translate to map patterns; students who have measured a 30° dip can visualise how that would appear as a V-pattern on a map.
- Graphic log construction in the field trains students to read vertical sequences; this directly prepares them for interpreting borehole logs and stratigraphic columns on the exam paper.
- Field sketching and annotated drawings develop the skill of extracting and labelling geological features — essential for annotating map extracts and cross-sections under exam conditions.
- Rose diagrams constructed from field joint measurements train students to recognise dominant structural trends; in the exam, rose diagrams appear as data to interpret rather than construct, but familiarity with the data type is necessary.
- Practising the geological code of conduct and safe working develops professional geological thinking that informs field-question answers about survey design.

Limitations:
- Fieldwork is centre-specific; the location, rock types and structures will differ from those on the exam map, so transferable skills matter more than site-specific knowledge.
- Time constraints mean that not every map skill can be directly practised in the field; some must also be practised through paper exercises.

Conclusion: Fieldwork is valuable because it develops the observational habits and spatial reasoning that underlie all map interpretation skills. However, its greatest contribution is building intuition about real geological structures rather than directly rehearsing exam tasks. Students who combine fieldwork experience with systematic map-reading practice are best prepared. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What does the rule of Vs tell you when a geological boundary forms a V-shape pointing upstream across a valley?
options: The strata are dipping upstream, against the valley gradient
The strata are horizontal or dipping gently downstream
The strata are vertical with no dip
The strata are overturned and dipping at more than 90°

knowledge_checks.q: Which principle of relative dating states that a fault cutting through bedding must have formed after the bedding?
A _____ is a scaled vertical column diagram showing the rock types and thicknesses encountered in a borehole or at an outcrop, using standard rock symbols.
The Geological Society's _____ of Conduct requires geologists to seek landowner permission, work safely and collect specimens minimally when undertaking fieldwork.
Match each fieldwork tool or technique to its primary purpose:
right: Measuring the dip angle and strike direction of a rock surface
Displaying the frequency of directional measurements on a circular plot
Recording rock types and thicknesses in a vertical borehole or outcrop sequence

flashcard_questions.q: What does the rule of Vs allow you to infer from a geological map?
flashcard_questions.a: The dip direction of strata, from the direction a V-shape points where a boundary crosses a valley.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a cross-section in geology?
flashcard_questions.a: A diagram showing the geology on a vertical slice through the ground along a chosen line on the map.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a graphic log used for?
flashcard_questions.a: Recording rock types and thicknesses to scale in a borehole or outcrop sequence using standard symbols.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a compass clinometer measure?
flashcard_questions.a: The dip angle and strike direction of rock surfaces such as bedding planes or fault planes.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a rose diagram show?
flashcard_questions.a: The frequency of directional measurements (e.g. joint orientations) in each compass direction, as petals.

flashcard_questions.q: What is geological history and how is it constructed from a map?
flashcard_questions.a: A chronological sequence of events, derived using superposition, cross-cutting relationships and unconformities.
A surface of erosion representing a gap in the geological record, where younger beds rest on older tilted ones.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three principles used to sequence geological events from a map?
Name three recording methods used during geological fieldwork.
flashcard_questions.a: Field sketch, annotated photograph, and graphic log.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Geological Code of Conduct?
flashcard_questions.a: Guidelines requiring geologists to get landowner permission, work safely and minimise specimen collection.

flashcard_questions.q: How many field occasions does the spec require before the examination?
flashcard_questions.a: Two field occasions, including at least one directed investigation.

glossary_terms.definition: A printed map showing the distribution of rock types and geological structures at the Earth's surface, simplified for exam use by reducing the number of rock units and removing minor features.
A diagram showing the geology as it would appear on a vertical slice through the ground along a chosen line, constructed from map patterns and dip data.
A chronological account of the geological events recorded in a sequence of rocks, derived by applying the principles of superposition, cross-cutting relationships and included fragments.
A vertical column diagram representing the sequence of rock types in a borehole or outcrop, with thickness drawn to scale, using standard symbols for each rock type.
A combined instrument used to measure the strike (horizontal compass direction of a rock surface) and dip (angle of inclination) of a rock plane such as a bedding surface or fault.
